nameStory: Henry's Elfin gets its name from its small, delicate size that evokes magical woodland creatures from folklore. The "elfin" butterflies are all tiny members of the hairstreak family, with wingspans that rarely exceed an inch. This particular species was named "Henry's" to honor an early lepidopterist, though it's also called the woodland elfin for its preference for forest edges and clearings.
description: Henry's Elfin is a small brown butterfly that belongs to the gossamer-winged butterfly family, known for their delicate, almost translucent wings. These tiny butterflies have a wingspan of about 0.75 to 1 inch, with rich brown wings marked by intricate patterns of lighter and darker bands. Like other hairstreaks, they have small tail-like projections on their hindwings and tend to hold their wings closed when at rest, showing off their beautifully patterned undersides. They're woodland butterflies that prefer forest edges and areas where their host plants grow.

idTips.label: Wing Position
idTips.description: Always rests with wings held vertically closed, never spreading them flat like many other butterflies - you'll rarely see the upper wing surfaces

idTips.label: Underwing Pattern
idTips.description: Hindwings show distinctive brown and white zigzag bands with a frosted appearance, often with small blue spots near the tiny tail projections

idTips.label: Size and Flight
idTips.description: Very small with quick, erratic flight pattern that seems almost bouncy - about the size of a penny when wings are spread

idTips.label: Tail Projections
idTips.description: Hindwings have small, thread-like tails that may be worn off in older individuals - these help confuse predators about which end is the head

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often seen perched on flowers with wings quivering slightly, and males establish territories by perching on shrubs and chasing away intruders

habitat: Henry's Elfin inhabits forest edges, woodland clearings, and areas where their host plants thrive, including both native and disturbed environments. In New England, look for them around holly bushes near the coast, redbud trees in inland areas, and increasingly around non-native buckthorn shrubs in various woodland settings. They prefer partly sunny locations with some shelter from wind, often near trails or forest openings where flowers provide nectar sources.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge in late April to early May and are most active during this season, when you'll see them flying around host plants and nectaring on spring flowers. This is the prime time to spot Henry's Elfin in New England.
seasonality.summer: By early summer, the adult flight period is usually over, and the species exists as eggs and developing caterpillars on host plants. You might find tiny caterpillars feeding on holly, redbud, or buckthorn leaves.
seasonality.fall: Caterpillars complete development and form chrysalises, spending the winter in this stage. No adult butterflies are visible, but you might spot the small, brown chrysalises attached to host plant stems.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as a chrysalis attached to host plant branches or nearby vegetation. The small, camouflaged chrysalis remains dormant until warm spring weather triggers emergence.

funFact: Henry's Elfin is actually expanding its range in New England thanks to invasive buckthorn - while most conservationists worry about invasive plants harming native species, this little butterfly has adapted to use the non-native shrub as a host plant, allowing its populations to grow in areas where it couldn't survive before.
confusionNotes: Henry's Elfin is easily confused with other elfin butterflies, especially Brown Elfin and Eastern Pine Elfin, since they're all small and brown. Look for Henry's Elfin's distinctive frosted or mottled underwing pattern with white zigzag markings - Brown Elfin lacks the white markings and has more uniform brown underwings, while Pine Elfin has bolder, more contrasting bands.
contextualKnowledge: The term "elfin" in butterfly names refers to their tiny size and delicate appearance, not any connection to mythology. These butterflies are part of a group that includes several similar-looking species, which can make field identification challenging even for experienced butterfly watchers.
compareHints: Among its elfin relatives, Henry's Elfin stands out with its mottled, frosted underwing appearance compared to the more uniform Brown Elfin or the boldly striped Eastern Pine Elfin. It's also distinguished by its diverse host plant preferences - while Pine Elfin sticks to pines and Brown Elfin prefers heath family plants, Henry's Elfin uses everything from holly to redbud to buckthorn. The white zigzag markings on the underwings are Henry's signature feature that separate it from its close cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its elfin relatives, the Eastern Pine Elfin is unique in its strong association with pine trees—other elfins like Brown Elfin prefer shrubs, while Henry's Elfin favors redbud and maple-leaved viburnum.

Among the elfin butterflies in New England, Brown Elfin is the most uniformly brown without distinctive markings - Eastern Pine Elfin has strong banding patterns, Frosted Elfin shows white frosting on wing edges, and Henry's Elfin displays that telltale white-edged line.

Among its elfin relatives, the Frosted Elfin is distinguished by its unique frosted appearance - Brown Elfins lack the white-gray markings and appear more uniformly brown, while Eastern Pine Elfins show stronger, more geometric patterns without the scattered frosted effect.
Among the green hairstreaks, the Juniper Hairstreak is distinguished by its habitat preference for dry areas with junipers, while Hessel's Hairstreak prefers wet cedar swamps.
Among its elfin relatives, the hoary elfin is distinguished by its silvery-gray coloration rather than the warmer browns of brown elfins or the orange-brown of Henry's elfins.

Bog elfins are distinguished from other Callophrys elfins primarily by habitat - while Brown Elfins and Eastern Pine Elfins prefer dry, upland areas with their respective host plants, bog elfins are wetland specialists.
